title: Being drafted: induction physical and a request to be stationed at 110th Street
summary: He didn't try to dodge; he had never been sick, passed the physical, and a friend arranged to have him at 110th Street, and he asked for the Army not the Navy.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Did you volunteer for the Army, or --

Oh, goodness no. Goodness, no. No. I didn't volunteer at all, not at all. The only thing I remember about the Army now, I had sense enough to know that, you know, you can't -- I mean you can't fight these things. If you have to go in the Army you have to go in the Army. And I wasn't about to harm myself trying, like a lot of the fellows when they were drafted, take drugs and you know, get full of whiskey or whatever, or eat soap, which they were doing. Well, see, that gave you a fast heartbeat. They were doing everything to try to keep out, to be rejected. So I said no. Then -- so then I said to myself, you know, after -- I said, yeah, I'll beat it. I said I'll beat it, and I did.
Oh, yeah. It's a long story. You want me to talk about the Army?

Well, anyway, I went down to the induction center, and of course they examine you and doctors on top of doctors, you know, from the top of your head to the bottom of your feet. It was a tremendous experience. I'd never been through it. In the first place I'd never had too many doctors in my whole life. Nothing had ever happened to
me. I didn't even have a cold. I didn't learn to blow my nose till I was about 21 or 22 years old. That's true.

And when I was a child everybody around me, all the children, had measles, smallpox, diphtheria. I never had anything. So when they got ahold of me I was perfect. Yeah, then I was inducted into the Army. But I remember the one thing that -- I had a friend who I had met up with, he's still my friend, incidentally. He's a big man in politics up in Boston. I just visited him a few months ago. He was already in the Army and he was stationed at 110th Street, you know, so he told me, he said, "Now, when you get your requisition --," is that what you call it? "Just tell me your number and your name and I'll get you here, on 110th Street." I said, "You mean it?" He said yeah. So I said, "Well, I'll do anything to be stationed at 110th Street. I'll even walk guard in front of the building." You know, they had -- it was like an installation, an Army installation. So I remember when they stamped my chart, bam, accepted. I said, well, that part of it's over. Now I can breathe easy. I'm accepted and that's the end of that. I'm accepted. You got accepted, what else can you do, you know? I'm not going to run out and jump in front of a subway train because I'm in the Army. But the thing that was uppermost in my mind was I prayed that they wouldn't put me in the Navy, because if I had to wear one of

those suits (Laughter) -- oh, gee. But then I came out. So on your way out of the induction center they have a Marine officer, a Naval officer and an Army officer, because they're going to give you a big hello and say, "Hey," and shake your hand. "How you doing?" You know. I said okay. Then they said to me, which was -- they said something to me real beautiful. They said, "Which branch of the service do you want to be in?" I already had my requisition on 110th Street and everything, you know. I said, "The Army. The Army." So I got in the Army.
